title: Revealing Structural and Optical Changes of Ammonia-Catalysts Under Realistic Reactor Conditions via Multimodal and in situ Electron Microscopy
content: U.S. primary chemical production emits over 186 million metric tons of greenhouse gases every year, contributing to ever-increasing global temperatures [1]. However, chemicals such as ammonia, methanol, and polymer precursors (ethylene) are necessary for feeding, powering, and clothing the world’s population. This struggle between global need and environmental cost is well exemplified in ammonia production, where 90% of all ammonia goes to make fertilizer for food but is simultaneously responsible for nearly 2% of all CO2 emissions [2]. To minimize environmental costs while maintaining the world’s population, we must develop more sustainable alternatives to ammonia production. Plasmonic photocatalysis harnesses light to generate highly energetic electrons that can drive reactions in a non-equilibrium state, avoiding the energy-expensive high pressures and temperatures required in traditional chemical synthesis. Recent work has demonstrated successful plasmonic ammonia synthesis at the reactor scale using bimetallic AuRu nanocatalysts [3], but much remains unknown about how these catalysts behave during active ammonia synthesis.
